digest.top_line: NRG/RTOG 0815: 6 mo STAD + dose-escalated RT in IR PCa, OS HR 0.87 (p=0.13) not met, but PSA failure HR 0.60 and DM HR 0.35.
digest.tldr: The common thread in prostate is choosing who gets ADT with RT. In IR disease, RTOG 0815 STAD cut DM but not OS. GC ≥0.45 (8% vs 1% 10-yr DM benefit), PAM50 Luminal B and pre-SRT PSA >0.5 flag who gains. In the GUAM Delphi, 76% of panelists favor moderate hypofx over SBRT at baseline IPSS 15-19.

sites.intro: Biomarker selection for ADT with definitive and salvage RT (GC, PAM50, MMAI, pre-RT PSA) led the day, alongside two GU-toxicity tools: a germline AE predictor and a Delphi consensus.

studies.name: RTOG 0815 — Decipher/GC Score Secondary Analysis
studies.tldr: Secondary analysis: adding STAD to RT cut 10-yr DM by 8% absolute in Int/High GC vs 1% in Low GC, intermediate-risk prostate.
details: 📊 Low GC (<0.45): 1% absolute 10-yr DM benefit from adding STAD
📊 Int/High GC (≥0.45): 8% absolute 10-yr DM benefit from adding STAD
📊 Benefit of STAD increased across the continuous GC spectrum (per slide)
🔍 Secondary analysis of NRG/RTOG 0815 RCT, intermediate-risk prostate, GC-profiled n=395
🔍 GC distribution: Low 44%, Intermediate 24%, High 32%
💊 STAD = short-term ADT added to RT; RT dose/fractionation not stated in source
⚠️ Biomarker subset of the parent trial; no interaction p-value or HR reported in source
⚠️ Low GC curves carry few DM events, so the 1% estimate is low-precision
🔗 Aligns with NRG GU010 (GUIDANCE), which tests GC-guided ADT omission in intermediate-risk disease

figures.caption: Predicted 10-yr DM by continuous GC score, RT + STAD vs RT alone.

verdict.rationale: Secondary biomarker analysis of a GC-profiled subset; prespecification and interaction statistics not reported in source. Hypothesis-generating for GC-guided ADT selection.
verdict.audience: Intermediate-risk prostate cancer, definitive RT candidates

studies.significance: Low GC was the largest group (44%), and adding STAD bought only 1% absolute 10-yr DM there, against 8% in Int/High GC. That puts RT alone on the table for nearly half of intermediate-risk men and points ADT toward the GC ≥0.45 group, the decision NRG GU010 is testing prospectively.
studies.monday_clinic: In intermediate-risk prostate cancer with a low Decipher/GC score (<0.45), this supports discussing RT without STAD; in Int/High GC it supports keeping STAD, and it does not address high-risk disease.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **Secondary analysis** of the NRG/RTOG 0815 randomized trial of RT ± short-term ADT (STAD). GC (Decipher) profiled in **n=395**.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: **Intermediate-risk** prostate cancer. GC distribution: Low (<0.45) 44%, Intermediate (0.45-0.6) 24%, High (>0.6) 32%.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Distant metastasis (DM)** at 10 yr, by GC stratum and across continuous GC score.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Absolute 10-yr DM benefit from STAD: **1% in Low GC** vs **8% in Int/High GC**. Predicted DM after RT alone rises with GC while staying low with RT + STAD.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: The parent RTOG 0815 tested STAD added to RT in intermediate risk; this analysis asks which GC stratum carries that benefit. NRG GU010 (GUIDANCE) is prospectively testing GC-guided ADT omission in this setting.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents intermediate-risk prostate cancer treated with definitive RT. Does not represent high-risk disease or pts without GC testing.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Few DM events in the Low GC stratum, so the 1% estimate is imprecise. No HR, CI, or interaction p-value in source.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: GC appears **predictive, not only prognostic**, for STAD benefit. Whether RT alone is safe for Low GC pts needs prospective confirmation.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Low GC was 44% of the cohort, and adding STAD gave only 1% absolute 10-yr DM benefit there vs 8% in Int/High GC. That puts RT alone on the table for nearly half of intermediate-risk men and points STAD toward GC ≥0.45.

open_questions: Is RT alone safe for low-GC intermediate-risk pts prospectively?
Does GC predict ADT benefit in high-risk disease?
Interaction p-value and HR by GC stratum

studies.name: NRG/RTOG 0815
studies.tldr: OS HR 0.87 (95% CI 0.72-1.04, p=0.13), not met; 6 mo STAD + dose-escalated RT cut PSA failure (HR 0.60) and DM (HR 0.35) in IR PCa.

details.text: 🔍 Ph 3 RCT, N=1493 (751 RT alone vs 742 RT + STAD); median f/u 10.3 y in survivors
🔍 RT: EBRT 79.2 Gy, or EBRT + LDR or HDR brachy boost; 89% received EBRT alone

details: 💊 STAD = 6 mo LHRH agonist + antiandrogen

details.text: 📐 Powered for 5-y OS 90% → 93% (HR 0.66), 85% power

details: 📊 Secondary disease-control and mortality endpoints
⚠️ 422 of 446 deaths were non-prostate cancer; competing mortality dilutes any OS signal

details.text: 📊 PSA failure benefit by subgroup (HR, STAD vs none)
subdetails: 1 IR factor: HR 0.66
2-3 IR factors: HR 0.52
EBRT: HR 0.58

details: ⚠️ Authors could not identify a subgroup that does not benefit; smaller subgroups had wide CIs

details.text: ⚠️ No PSMA PET, genomic classifier, or MMAI selection; 67% had a single IR factor

figures.caption: Schema: dose-escalated EBRT (79.2 Gy), EBRT + LDR boost, or EBRT + HDR boost ± 6 months androgen blockade.

verdict.rationale: Adequately powered phase 3 with long follow-up; OS primary not met, but consistent disease-control benefit supports selective STAD as a toxicity trade-off rather than an OS gain.
verdict.audience: Non-metastatic intermediate-risk prostate cancer, dose-escalated RT, median age 68

studies.significance: Dose escalation did not erase the ADT benefit: with 79.2 Gy or a brachy boost, STAD still cut distant mets (40 vs 14 events, HR 0.35) and PCSM (HR 0.26). OS stayed flat because 422 of 446 deaths were non-prostate cancer, so the STAD call is a disease-control vs QoL/cardiac trade-off, not a survival one.
studies.monday_clinic: In non-metastatic intermediate-risk prostate cancer planned for dose-escalated EBRT or brachy boost, this supports discussing 6 mo STAD for fewer relapses and PC deaths without an OS promise; it does not identify which IR subgroup can safely omit it.

primary_endpoint.name: Overall survival
primary_endpoint.stat_detail: 95% CI 0.72-1.04, p=0.13; did not meet OS

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Phase III prospective randomized trial, **N=1493** (751 vs 742). Median follow-up 9.4 y overall, **10.3 y in survivors**. Stratified by number of IR factors, ACE-27 comorbidity, and RT modality.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: **Non-metastatic intermediate-risk** prostate cancer with ≥1 of Gleason 7, PSA >10 but ≤20 ng/mL, or cT2b-T2c; all 3 factors plus ≥50% positive cores excluded. Median age 68, median PSA 8.1 ng/mL, 92% Gleason 7, 67% single IR factor.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: **Dose-escalated EBRT to 79.2 Gy**, or EBRT with an LDR or HDR brachytherapy boost; **89% received EBRT alone**. More than 90% of contours and dose analyses scored per protocol or acceptable variation.

analysis_sections.label: Regimen
analysis_sections.body: **6 months STAD**: LHRH agonist plus antiandrogen. LHRH compliance 91%, antiandrogen 87%.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Primary: OS**, powered for 5-y OS 90% to 93% (HR 0.66). Secondary: biochemical failure, local failure, distant metastasis, PC death, salvage therapy, non-PC death.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: **OS not improved** (HR 0.87, p=0.13); PSA failure, MFS, distant mets, salvage ADT and PC deaths all favored STAD, with **non-PC mortality similar** (HR 0.93).

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: Overall grade 3+ late AEs similar (HR 1.08), but **metabolic, sexual and cardiac grade 3+ events higher with STAD**. EPIC hormone and sexual domains dropped early with STAD and **largely converged by 60 months**; urinary and bowel domains similar.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: RTOG 9408 established STAD with RT at conventional doses; 0815 asks whether **dose-escalated RT removes that need**, and the disease-control answer is no. The OS answer differs because the population is IR with high competing mortality.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents non-metastatic intermediate-risk prostate cancer treated with dose-escalated EBRT or brachy boost, mostly single IR factor, conventionally staged. Does not represent PSMA PET-staged, genomic-classifier-selected, or high-risk disease.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: OS power assumption ignored the **competing non-PC mortality** that dominated deaths. Brachy-boost and multi-factor subsets are small, so **subgroup omission cannot be defended** from this trial.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: STAD buys **durable disease control and fewer PC deaths** without excess non-PC mortality, at a transient QoL cost. The open question is selection: which IR pts can skip it, which the authors defer to imaging, genomics, and MMAI.

studies.interpretation:
The cleanest way to read 0815 is as two separate answers to two questions the trial was not designed to separate. The question it was powered for, whether 6 months of ADT improves survival when the radiation dose is already escalated, gets a negative answer. The question most radiation oncologists actually care about, whether dose escalation makes ADT redundant for disease control, gets an equally clear answer in the other direction: PSA failure, distant metastasis, salvage ADT and prostate cancer death all moved in favor of STAD, with an HR of 0.35 for distant metastasis and 0.26 for prostate cancer death.

The OS miss is largely structural. The trial was designed around a 5-year OS improvement from 90% to 93%, an assumption that implicitly treated prostate cancer as a meaningful driver of death in an intermediate-risk, median-age-68 population. It was not: 422 of 446 deaths were from other causes. With prostate cancer deaths of 19 versus 5, no plausible effect on cancer mortality could have surfaced as a significant all-cause signal. The reassuring companion finding is that non-prostate cancer mortality was not higher with STAD (HR 0.93), which matters because the historical worry about ADT in older men with comorbidity is cardiovascular harm. The grade 3+ cardiac excess (26 vs 10 events) is real but did not translate into excess non-cancer death at this follow-up.

Against RTOG 9408, which supported adding STAD at conventional doses, 0815 is better read as continuity than reversal. The argument that higher local dose would close the gap is weakened by the distant metastasis result: ADT appears to act on occult systemic disease that local dose cannot address. That said, distant metastasis events were few in absolute terms, 40 versus 14 across nearly 1,500 men, so the relative effect is large while the absolute stakes for a typical patient are modest.

The selection question is where the trial leaves the reader short. Two thirds had a single intermediate-risk factor, 89% received EBRT alone, and staging predates PSMA PET and routine genomic classifiers. Subgroup HRs for PSA failure all favored STAD, but the authors state they could not identify a group that does not benefit, which is not the same as showing all groups benefit; the brachy-boost and multi-factor strata are too small to support either claim. Practices that already individualize by unfavorable versus favorable intermediate-risk features will find nothing here that forbids it, and nothing that validates it.

The practical upshot is that STAD in this setting should be framed as a trade: fewer relapses, less salvage therapy and fewer prostate cancer deaths, against early sexual and hormonal QoL deterioration that largely recovered by 60 months and an excess of cardiac and metabolic events. For a patient whose competing mortality is high, that trade looks thin; for a fit patient with a long horizon, the reduction in distant metastasis and salvage ADT carries more weight. The trial would be wrong in its disease-control conclusions only if antiandrogen non-compliance or modality imbalance biased the secondary endpoints, and neither appears large enough to do so.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Dose escalation to 79.2 Gy or brachy boost did not replace STAD for disease control: distant mets HR 0.35, PSA failure HR 0.60. OS stayed flat because 422 of 446 deaths were non-prostate cancer, so the ADT decision with dose-escalated RT is a disease-control vs QoL trade-off.

open_questions: Which intermediate-risk subgroups can safely omit STAD?
Does PSMA PET or genomic selection amplify STAD benefit?

studies.name: NRG/RTOG 0534 SPPORT — PAM50 Analysis
studies.tldr: PAM50 Luminal B vs non-Luminal B: STADT with salvage RT added 31% vs 10% 5-y FFP (p-int=.01); 10-y MFS benefit 20% vs -3% (p-int=.05).

details.text: 📊 Absolute benefit from postop STADT by PAM50 subtype

details: 🔍 Tissue biomarker analysis of SPPORT (Pollack, Lancet Onc 2022); analytic cohort n=709 of 1792 enrolled

details.text: 🔍 Sample attrition from n=1039 with banked tissue
subdetails: Insufficient RNA: n=3
Failed cDNA QC: n=120
Failed microarray QC: n=207

details: 📊 Luminal B framed as both prognostic and predictive of postop ADT benefit
📊 Per-arm slide: PLNRT + PBRT + STADT vs PBRT alone HR 0.40, p=0.004 in one subtype panel; subtype and endpoint labels not legible in OCR
⚠️ PLNRT vs PBRT + STADT (arm 3 vs 2) HR 0.64, p=0.16 in that panel; nodal-field effect by subtype unresolved from source
⚠️ MFS interaction borderline (p=.05); CIs for absolute benefits not reported in source
⚠️ RT dose, target definition and ADT duration not stated in source

figures.caption: FFP by PAM50 subtype. PBRT + STADT +/- PLNRT vs PBRT alone: HR 0.34 (0.23-0.52), p<0.001. Interaction P=0.01.
Post-RP, PSA 0.1-2.0 ng/mL, Gleason ≤9. Enrolled n=1792; analytic cohort n=709: PBRT alone n=215, PBRT + STADT n=247, PBRT + STADT + PLNRT n=247.

verdict.rationale: Secondary tissue-subset analysis (709/1792) of a completed RCT; prespecification not stated, MFS interaction borderline, no independent validation cohort in source.
verdict.audience: Post-RP PSA 0.1-2.0 ng/mL, pT2/pT3 N0M0, Gleason ≤9, salvage RT

studies.significance: The ADT add-on to prostate-bed RT concentrates in Luminal B: 31% vs 10% absolute 5-y FFP gain, and the 10-y MFS gain (20%) vanishes outside Luminal B (-3%). Whether subtype also sorts pelvic nodal RT benefit is unsettled; the per-arm panels lack legible subtype labels in source.
studies.monday_clinic: In post-RP salvage RT candidates with PSA 0.1-2.0 ng/mL, a PAM50 Luminal B call strengthens the case for adding short-term ADT; it does not yet support omitting ADT in non-Luminal B pts, who still gained 10% 5-y FFP.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: PAM50 molecular subtyping of banked tissue from NRG/RTOG 0534 SPPORT (Pollack, Lancet Onc 2022). **Analytic cohort n=709** of 1792 enrolled; subtype tested for prognostic and predictive value against randomised arm.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: **Post-RP, PSA 0.1-2.0 ng/mL, pT2 or pT3 N0M0, Gleason ≤9.** Limited to pts with tissue passing RNA, cDNA and microarray QC.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Three arms: **PBRT alone** (n=215), **PBRT + STADT** (n=247), **PBRT + STADT + PLNRT** (n=247). Dose and target definition not stated in source.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: FFP and MFS, with subtype-by-treatment interaction tests.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: STADT benefit larger in Luminal B on both FFP (**p-int=.01**) and MFS (**p-int=.05**); per-subtype absolute benefits in the details table.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: SPPORT and RTOG 9601 established adding hormone therapy to salvage RT without biomarker selection. Decipher analyses of RTOG 9601 previously tested genomic selection for that decision; PAM50 is a different, subtype-based axis.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents post-RP pT2/pT3 N0M0 pts with PSA 0.1-2.0 ng/mL receiving prostate-bed salvage RT. Does not represent node-positive disease, PSMA-staged populations, or ARSI intensification.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: MFS interaction sits at the threshold, and CIs on absolute benefits are not in source. RT dose, ADT duration and nodal-field effect by subtype cannot be read from the slides.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: Luminal B looks like the subtype where ADT earns its toxicity in salvage RT, and the **MFS signal disappears outside it**. It does not settle de-escalation in non-Luminal B pts, where FFP gain persisted.

studies.interpretation:
The clinical question here is a familiar one for anyone giving salvage radiotherapy after prostatectomy: SPPORT and RTOG 9601 both support adding hormone therapy to prostate-bed RT, yet many pts at the lower end of the PSA range gain little and absorb the toxicity anyway. Genomic selection has been the obvious answer, and the Decipher analyses of RTOG 9601 made the first serious attempt. PAM50 brings a different biology to the same decision. Rather than a risk score, it assigns an intrinsic subtype, and the hypothesis carried over from earlier retrospective post-prostatectomy work is that luminal B tumours are androgen-receptor driven in a way that makes them unusually sensitive to castration.

The result is internally coherent. Luminal B pts gained 31% absolute 5-y FFP from short-term ADT versus 10% in everyone else, with an interaction p of .01, and on the harder endpoint the gap widens rather than closes: 20% versus -3% at 10 years for MFS. That pattern matters more than either number alone. A biomarker that separates benefit on a PSA-driven endpoint but not on metastasis would be telling us mostly about biochemical kinetics. Here the non-luminal B group appears to get a biochemical delay without a metastatic payoff, which is exactly what a reader worried about overtreatment wants to see.

The confidence adjustment runs in the other direction on several fronts. Only 709 of 1792 enrolled pts contributed, after tissue availability and three separate QC losses, so the analytic cohort is a selected subset of a randomised trial rather than the trial itself. The MFS interaction lands at p=.05, which is a threshold result, not a margin. The source gives no confidence intervals on the absolute benefits, and a -3% point estimate in a subgroup this size is compatible with a modest benefit. Whether the analysis was prespecified is not stated.

For a radiation oncologist, the nodal question is the unfinished piece. The per-arm slide shows one subtype panel where PLNRT plus PBRT plus STADT beat PBRT alone (HR 0.40, p=0.004) while the arm 3 versus arm 2 comparison was not significant (HR 0.64, p=0.16), but the subtype labels are not legible in the captured text, so it cannot be said which biology drives any pelvic-field signal. The headline answers the ADT question, not the target-volume one.

What would make this wrong: failure to replicate in an independent salvage cohort, or attenuation once PSMA PET staging removes occult nodal disease that may currently be inflating ADT benefit in some subgroups. Until then it is a credible selection hypothesis for adding ADT in luminal B tumours, and a weak basis for withholding it from the rest.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: ADT benefit with prostate-bed salvage RT concentrates in Luminal B (31% vs 10% 5-y FFP). Whether subtype also sorts pelvic nodal RT benefit is unresolved; per-arm panels lack legible subtype labels in source.
significance_by_specialty.medonc: PAM50 Luminal B marks the hormonally responsive salvage pts: 10-y MFS gain from STADT 20% vs -3% outside Luminal B (p-int=.05). It is a candidate selector for ADT, not yet a basis for withholding it.

open_questions: Does PAM50 Luminal B also select for pelvic nodal RT benefit?
Does non-Luminal B status justify omitting ADT with salvage RT?
Independent validation in another salvage RT cohort

studies.name: PROSTOX Ultra (SCIMITAR/EXCALIBUR)
studies.tldr: Continuous AUC 0.814 and 0.824 for late G2+ GU AE after post-op prostate-bed SBRT; the intact 0.50 cutoff fails post-op, and a recalibrated 0.25 cutoff gives a pooled AUC of 0.748.

details.text: 🔍 32-mirSNP germline signature, originally built on intact-prostate SBRT with a prespecified 0.50 threshold

details: 🔍 Tested in 2 prospective post-op SBRT cohorts using the original intact-prostate model, no redevelopment
🔍 Saliva germline DNA, CLIA-certified lab

details.text: 📊 Discrimination for late G2+ GU AE by cohort

rows: Median score, AE vs no AE

details.text: 📊 Pooled AUC at 0.25 was 0.748 (fixed-effects meta-analysis, 1,000 bootstrap iterations)
📐 Candidate post-op thresholds ~0.10-0.31 met sensitivity >=0.65 and specificity >=0.70; 0.25 selected

details: 📊 Age, baseline pad use, IPSS, and RP-to-SBRT interval did not predict toxicity (all p > 0.2)

details.text: ⚠️ The 0.25 threshold was chosen in the same cohorts it was tested on, so AUC at 0.25 is optimistic

details: ⚠️ Conference abstract via trade press; follow-up duration and GU AE grading scale not reported in source

verdict.rationale: Post-hoc biomarker validation in two modest post-op cohorts; the 0.25 threshold was derived and tested on the same data, and no prospective test of score-guided management exists.
verdict.audience: Post-RP pts receiving 5-fx prostate-bed SBRT ± pelvic nodes

studies.significance: The intact 0.50 cutoff cannot be reused after prostatectomy. In SCIMITAR it caught only 0.546 of toxicity cases, and in EXCALIBUR every pt with toxicity scored below it. Age, pad use, IPSS and the RP-to-SBRT interval did not predict late G2+ GU AE (all p > 0.2). That leaves the germline score as the only stratifier here for counseling before 5-fx prostate-bed SBRT.
studies.monday_clinic: In a post-RP pt being considered for 5-fraction prostate-bed SBRT, a PROSTOX Ultra report read against the intact 0.50 cutoff likely under-calls late GU toxicity risk. The 0.25 post-op cutoff is exploratory, and the data do not extend to conventionally fractionated salvage RT.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Biomarker validation of **PROSTOX Ultra** in two prospective post-op SBRT cohorts, **SCIMITAR (NCT03541850)** and **EXCALIBUR (NCT04915508)**. Discrimination was assessed with continuous AUC and with dichotomized performance at the intact **0.50** threshold, followed by exploratory threshold recalibration.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: SCIMITAR enrolled **100 post-prostatectomy pts** (89 evaluable), and EXCALIBUR contributed **74 evaluable** pts. Baseline pad use and IPSS were recorded.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: SCIMITAR delivered **30-34 Gy in 5 fractions** to the prostate bed ± pelvic nodes. EXCALIBUR used **5-fraction SBRT** to the prostate bed ± nodes; its dose is not stated in source.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Late grade 2+ GU adverse events**, analyzed by continuous AUC, AUC at a threshold, sensitivity and specificity. AUCs were bootstrapped and pooled by fixed-effects meta-analysis.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Risk ordering held as a continuous score in both cohorts, while binary performance depended on the threshold chosen. At the recalibrated **0.25** cutoff the **pooled AUC was 0.748**.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: In intact-prostate SBRT the signature was validated at a **0.50** threshold. Post-op, the same genetic ordering persists but the decision trigger shifts **downward**, so the intact cutoff does not transfer.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents post-RP pts receiving 5-fraction prostate-bed SBRT with or without pelvic nodes. Does not represent conventionally fractionated or moderately hypofractionated post-op RT, or intact-prostate treatment.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: The **0.25 threshold was selected and evaluated in the same cohorts**, with no held-out validation. EXCALIBUR's event count and sensitivity are not reported in source.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The post-op bed appears to carry a **lower toxicity threshold** for the same germline risk, which fits a GU tract already stressed by surgery. Whether score-guided planning (dose, nodal coverage, fractionation choice) lowers late GU AE is untested.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The intact 0.50 cutoff cannot be reused after prostatectomy. In SCIMITAR it caught only 0.546 of toxicity cases, and in EXCALIBUR every pt with toxicity scored below it. Clinical factors did not predict late G2+ GU AE (all p > 0.2), leaving the germline score as the only stratifier here for counseling before 5-fx prostate-bed SBRT.

open_questions: Does the 0.25 post-op threshold hold in an independent cohort?
Does score-guided planning reduce late GU toxicity after prostate-bed SBRT?
Does the signature apply to conventionally fractionated post-op RT?

studies.name: GUAM Working Group — International Consensus Guideline on GU AEs

details: ⚠️ No dose-volume constraint reached consensus

details.text: ⚠️ Panel radonc-weighted (34 of 48)

verdict.rationale: Modified Delphi over a 183-article review; outputs are panel agreement, not outcomes. RT-specific trial evidence is thin for most medications recommended.
verdict.audience: Prostate RT pts with acute or late GU AEs, intact or post-RP

studies.significance: No bladder or urethral dose-volume constraint reached consensus, so the technique lever left is margin: MIRAGE MRI-guided 2-mm margins cut late G≥2 GU AEs 51% → 27% vs CT-guided 4-mm. The IPSS ≥20 outlet-procedure referral (74%) and SBRT after an outlet procedure (52%) fall below the panel's own 75% bar.
studies.monday_clinic: In an intact-prostate pt with baseline IPSS 15-19 weighing SBRT vs moderate hypofractionation, panel opinion (76%) favors moderate hypofx; it does not settle SBRT eligibility after an outlet procedure, where agreement was 52%.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Systematic review (**183 articles**) plus a **3-round modified Delphi**, May 2025 to Feb 2026. **48 experts** from 15 countries (34 radonc, 7 medonc, 7 urologic oncologists); consensus = **≥75% agreement**. Endorsed by ASTRO and ESTRO.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Men receiving prostate RT with acute or late GU AEs, split by **intact prostate vs post-prostatectomy** and, if intact, **obstructive vs irritative** symptoms. Recommendations assume UTI and other causes are excluded first.

analysis_sections.label: Regimen
analysis_sections.body: Intact obstructive: **alpha blocker 1L**. Intact irritative and post-prostatectomy: **anti-spasmodic 1L**. 80% against prophylaxis before symptom onset; 80% add a 2nd agent rather than switch.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: **76% favor moderate hypofx over SBRT at baseline IPSS 15-19**; 85% recommend a full bladder at simulation and treatment. **No dose-volume constraint reached consensus.** After an outlet procedure, 94% wait ≥8 wk and 66% ≥12 wk before RT.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Margin reduction is anchored in MIRAGE: MRI-guided 2-mm margins lowered late G≥2 GU AEs from **51% to 27%** vs CT-guided 4-mm. CHHiP, PROFIT, RTOG 0415 and the HYDRA meta-analysis are cited as showing no consistent late GU AE increase with moderate hypofx.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents men with GU AEs from prostate RT, intact prostate or post-prostatectomy. Does not represent urinary symptoms from UTI or other non-RT causes, which must be excluded first.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Several reported items fall **below the 75% threshold** (postop alpha blocker 74%, IPSS ≥20 referral 74%, SBRT post-procedure 52%), so not every stated position is consensus. Panel is radonc-weighted, and urethral contouring reliability is flagged as unresolved.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: Replaces extrapolation from BPH and overactive-bladder data with an RT-specific framework, but the evidence base for most medications remains non-RT. Framed as a **living document**; BEFORE, RadTARGET, RELIEF and DESTINATION-2 are ongoing.

studies.interpretation:
The value of this document is less any single recommendation than the fact that it exists. Management of GU toxicity after prostate RT has been borrowed wholesale from BPH and overactive-bladder practice, and the panel says as much. What it offers is a structured default sequence that separates obstructive from irritative symptoms and intact from post-prostatectomy anatomy, which is the distinction most clinics already make informally but rarely write down. A radiation oncologist reading it should treat the medication algorithm as codified habit rather than tested evidence: the presenters themselves list RT-specific support for commonly used drugs as an open gap.

The more consequential content for an RT reader is the fractionation and technique section. The IPSS-based steer away from SBRT toward moderate hypofractionation at baseline IPSS 15-19 reflects a widely held instinct, and 76% agreement clears the bar. But the threshold itself was not unanimous: answers spread from 10-14 through ≥25, and the modal band drew 61%. A reader should take the 15-19 cutoff as a reasonable anchor, not a validated boundary. The panel leans on CHHiP, PROFIT, RTOG 0415 and the HYDRA meta-analysis to argue moderate hypofractionation does not consistently add late GU toxicity, which is what makes it the safer harbor for a symptomatic gland.

The most actionable comparative point is margins. MIRAGE, with late G≥2 GU AEs of 51% vs 27% for CT-guided 4-mm vs MRI-guided 2-mm margins, is the one randomized technique result cited, and it matters precisely because no bladder or urethral dose-volume constraint reached consensus. In the absence of an agreed constraint, margin and image guidance are the levers a planner can defend. That is a narrow evidentiary base for a technique recommendation, and the unresolved reliability of urethral contouring limits how far urethra-sparing approaches can be codified.

Methodologically, readers should check each item's agreement figure against the ≥75% definition. Several positions reported in the presentation fall short: the post-prostatectomy alpha blocker item at 74%, referral for an outlet procedure at IPSS ≥20 at 74%, waiting ≥12 weeks after an outlet procedure at 66%, and SBRT after an outlet procedure at 52%. These read as majority opinion, not consensus, and the last is close to an even split. The panel is also weighted toward radiation oncologists (34 of 48), which may shape where procedural thresholds landed relative to what urologists alone would set.

The framework would be wrong where its extrapolations are wrong: if alpha blockers or anti-spasmodics behave differently in irradiated tissue, or if SBRT tolerance at moderate baseline IPSS proves better than the panel assumes. The ongoing BEFORE, RadTARGET, RELIEF and DESTINATION-2 trials, and the stated plan to update it as a living document, are where those assumptions get tested.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: No bladder or urethral dose-volume constraint reached consensus, leaving margin as the defensible lever: MIRAGE MRI-guided 2-mm margins cut late G≥2 GU AEs 51% → 27% vs CT-guided 4-mm. Moderate hypofx over SBRT at IPSS 15-19 cleared consensus at 76%; SBRT after an outlet procedure (52%) did not.

studies.significance: The ADT decision with salvage RT now has three selectors, one of them randomized: PSA above 0.50 ng/mL (POSEIDON HR 0.72 and 0.69), PAM50 luminal B (GU006 MFS HR 0.27) and MMAI-high. Adverse pathology count did not modify benefit (interaction p=0.40). Margin, SVI or ECE alone should not drive ADT addition at low pre-RT PSA.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Trade-press summary of an invited ASTRO 2026 talk. It pulls together **two IPD meta-analyses**, the **biomarker-stratified NRG GU006 RCT**, post-hoc PAM50 and MMAI analyses of RTOG 9601/0534, and the planned NRG SYMPHONY trials.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: POSEIDON: adding hormone therapy to post-op RT did not significantly improve OS overall (**HR 0.87, p=0.06**), but benefit appeared **above PSA 0.50 ng/mL**. In GU006, apalutamide benefit was **confined to luminal B** (5-yr MFS 95% vs 82%); non-luminal B got none (90% vs 89%).

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: GU006 prospectively tests the luminal-basal ADT-response hypothesis from the 2017 JAMA Oncol PAM50 work, and the post-hoc RTOG 0534 PAM50 analysis points the same way. Decipher validation in post-op cohorts (RTOG 9601, RTOG 0534, NRG GU002, NRG GU006) is prognostic. **PAM50 is the one presented as predictive** (labelled a level 1A predictive biomarker).

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: MMAI benefit separation is reported as approximate curve readings (**~40% vs ~20%**) without HRs or interaction tests in the source. The RTOG 0534 PAM50 data are retrospective, and the source does not map each HR to its arm comparison.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The talk argues for **biology-selected intensification**: pathology tells you who relapses, not who benefits from ADT. Open is whether PAM50 and MMAI agree on the same pts and how either interacts with PSA level.

studies.interpretation:
The argument Spratt builds is that the post-prostatectomy ADT question has been asked at the wrong level of resolution. At the population level, POSEIDON's pooled answer is a non-significant OS signal for adding hormone therapy (HR 0.87, p=0.06) and nothing for extending it to 24 months (HR 0.96). A reader could take that as permission to drop ADT from salvage RT. The PSA-stratified data argue against a flat reading. The HR moves from 1.14 at PSA ≤0.20 to 0.72 and 0.69 above 0.50 ng/mL, a gradient consistent with ADT acting on disease burden beyond the prostate bed. That fits the clinical intuition that a higher pre-SRT PSA signals occult disease the RT field may not cover. The caveat is that PSA strata in an IPD meta-analysis are subgroups. Their gradient is persuasive, but trials with different eras, PSA eligibility and ADT agents were pooled to get it.

The adverse-feature analysis is arguably the more practice-relevant negative. Many clinicians use positive margins, SVI or high grade to justify ADT at salvage. The IPD data show these features predict worse OS and MFS but do not modify hormone-therapy benefit (OS interaction p=0.40). That separates prognosis from prediction, which is the right frame. It also means a pathology-heavy, low-PSA pt is not, on this evidence, an ADT candidate by default.

GU006 is the strongest piece because it is the only prospective, placebo-controlled, biomarker-stratified randomization in the set. The luminal B signal holds on MFS, not just biochemical control, which matters because bPFS gains from short androgen blockade are expected and not always meaningful. Two things should temper confidence. The luminal B MFS interval runs from 0.07 to 0.95, so the point estimate of 0.27 rests on few events. And the non-luminal B bPFS estimate is reported with an 80% CI, which says something about how the trial was powered for that stratum. Calling PAM50 a level 1A predictive biomarker on one trial plus a post-hoc confirmation is a strong claim. Replication, and agreement between PAM50 and genomic or MMAI risk in the same pts, would firm it up.

The MMAI data are the least mature for decision use. The development path skipped steps that Decipher went through, and the treatment-benefit separation is presented as approximate 12-year risks rather than interaction estimates. MMAI-high pts appeared to halve distant metastasis with hormone therapy, while MMAI-low curves overlapped. That is hypothesis-strengthening, not yet a selector to act on alone.

For the RT reader, SYMPHONY is where the field tests the volume and dose dimensions this talk mostly leaves aside: 5-fraction prostate bed SBRT, reduced-dose RT, and elective nodal coverage at salvage. If biomarker and PSMA selection are built into those randomizations, the next decade's salvage decisions may be made on biology rather than on clinical risk tiers.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Pathology risk (margin, SVI, ECE, GG4-5) did not modify hormone-therapy benefit with post-op RT (interaction p=0.40), so it should not drive ADT addition alone. SYMPHONY will randomize 5-fx prostate bed SBRT, reduced dose and elective nodal RT at salvage.
significance_by_specialty.medonc: GU006 restricts the apalutamide benefit with salvage RT to PAM50 luminal B (5-yr MFS 95% vs 82%, HR 0.27). Non-luminal B pts gained nothing (90% vs 89%). Extending ADT from 4-6 to 24 mo did not improve OS (HR 0.96).

open_questions: Does PAM50 luminal B status replicate as predictive in another randomized trial?
Do PAM50 and MMAI select the same pts for ADT?
Does 5-fraction prostate bed SBRT match conventional salvage RT?
